title: Patch Conversions
execute:
  warning: false
---

DASCore converts patches to common library objects and back.


## [Pandas](https://pandas.pydata.org/)

```python
import dascore as dc

patch = dc.get_example_patch()

df = patch.io.to_dataframe()
patch_from_df = dc.io.dataframe_to_patch(df)
```

## [Xarray](https://docs.xarray.dev/)

```python
import dascore as dc

patch = dc.get_example_patch()

dar = patch.io.to_xarray()
patch_from_dar = dc.io.xarray_to_patch(dar)
```

Coordinate labels are materialized, as in any xarray index. With `lazy_coords=True` (or a collection of names) the DataArray's index instead holds the patch's own coordinate and computes labels only for the samples a selection or `.values` asks about. Selection answers as it does on a materialized index (partial datetime strings, `method="nearest"`, `tolerance`), and converting back returns the coordinate exactly, fractional sampling rates and gaps included.

```python
import dascore as dc

patch = dc.get_example_patch()

lazy = patch.io.to_xarray(lazy_coords=True)
```

From xarray 2026.9 a lazy array combines with an array whose index holds its labels (built from numpy, loaded from netCDF, or converted with the default) when the labels are equal, though the comparison reads every lazy label. Labels that differ, reindexing to new labels, and any such mix on earlier xarray raise an `AlignmentError`. To combine them, give the lazy array ordinary indexes: `drop_indexes` removes the lazy index but keeps the coordinate's labels, and `set_xindex` builds an ordinary index from them, reading every label into memory (8 bytes a sample; a day at 1 kHz is about 0.7 GB). The data stays as it is. Select first where you can, so only the selection's labels are read:

```python
eager = lazy.drop_indexes(["time", "distance"]).set_xindex("time").set_xindex("distance")
```

Where the labels differ, or on xarray before 2026.9, the other way round often costs less: give the ordinary array the lazy index type instead. Its labels are already in memory, and where the two are the same coordinate (one a selection of the other, say) they align without reading the lazy labels at all; equal labels stated another way, or labels that differ, are joined as ordinary indexes would be, which reads both.

```python
from dascore.xarray.index import CoordIndex

aligned = eager.drop_indexes("time").set_xindex("time", CoordIndex)
```

A whole spool converts to a lazy, [dask](https://docs.dask.org/)-backed [DataTree](https://docs.xarray.dev/en/stable/user-guide/hierarchical-data.html) with one node per group of related patches (partitioned exactly as [`chunk`](`dascore.Spool.chunk`) partitions them) and one child node per merged output segment. Building the tree reads no data, and the coordinate of the dimension segments are merged along is lazy (as with `lazy_coords=True` above), so a segment spanning years of samples costs nothing to label. Other dimensions keep ordinary indexes, so per-channel arrays such as gains combine with a segment directly; along the merged dimension, use the `drop_indexes`/`set_xindex` swap above. Computing a selection loads only the source patches it touches. A local file which changed since the spool was indexed is refused when the tree is built, and one changed afterwards when a read finds it the wrong shape; run `spool.update()` and convert again.

```python
import dascore as dc

spool = dc.get_example_spool("diverse_das")

# Convert the spool to a DataTree of lazy arrays.
tree = spool.io.to_xarray()

# Nothing has been loaded yet; this reads only the patches it needs.
first = next(node for node in tree.subtree if "data" in node.dataset)
small = first.dataset["data"].isel(time=slice(0, 100)).compute()
```

A selection reads only the samples it names, however large the files behind it are. `block_size` bounds a bulk read instead: computing a whole segment asks for one block at a time, so a source patch larger than it is read in several windows rather than whole. Unset, it takes the configured `xarray_block_size` (256 MiB by default). A format which cannot hand back a window reads whole whatever the setting says, since splitting it would read the file once per block.

### Patch methods on a DataArray

A DataArray DASCore produced carries a `dc` accessor holding every public `Patch` method. A call converts to a patch, runs the method, and converts a patch it returns back; a result which is not a patch, such as an array or a spool, comes back as it is. A method taking another patch takes another DataArray.

```python
import dascore as dc

dar = dc.get_example_patch().io.to_xarray()

filtered = dar.dc.pass_filter(time=(1, 10))
times = dar.dc.get_array("time")
patch = dar.dc.to_patch()
```

A DataArray from somewhere else needs `import dascore.xarray.accessor` first, since registering the accessor means importing xarray, which DASCore does not do on its own.

A dask-backed DataArray is passed through as it stands, so a method which works on the array's own backend leaves it lazy. One which cannot converts, as it does on a patch. Where such a method announces that conversion, and the array is larger than free memory, the accessor raises rather than attempting it; a method which converts silently is not caught, and fails on memory as it would anywhere else.

A coordinate a DataArray states rather than stores (a lazy one, whose labels are computed on demand) is stated again in what a method hands back, so labelling a long acquisition costs no more after a call than before it. Every DataArray in the call says how its own coordinates arrived, an argument as much as the one called on. A coordinate which arrived spelled out anywhere is spelled out in the result, since a spelled-out index is what xarray aligns on. Laziness follows the name, so a method which renames such a coordinate spells its labels out under the new name.

## [ObsPy](https://docs.obspy.org/)

```python
import dascore as dc

patch = dc.get_example_patch()

stream = patch.io.to_obspy()
patch_from_stream = dc.io.obspy_to_patch(stream)
```

:::{.callout-note}
`obspy_to_patch` requires every trace to have the same data length and the requested dimension in `stats` (`distance` by default).
:::

## Research HDF5 arrays

An HDF5 array with timing and spacing attributes may need an explicit mapping when it lacks the units required by a reader. For example, the [Taiwan MiDAS release](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.15241981) includes `original_foreshock.h5`, with a channel-by-time `data` array and `begin_time`, `dt_s`, and `dx_m` attributes, but no data units. After downloading that file, this example reads its first 1,000 time samples and converts them through xarray:

```{python}
#| eval: false
import h5py
import numpy as np
import xarray as xr

import dascore as dc

with h5py.File("original_foreshock.h5", "r") as source:
    dataset = source["data"]
    values = dataset[:, :1000]
    start = dc.to_datetime64(dataset.attrs["begin_time"])
    interval = dc.to_timedelta64(float(dataset.attrs["dt_s"]))
    spacing = float(dataset.attrs["dx_m"])

array = xr.DataArray(
    values,
    dims=("distance", "time"),
    coords={
        "time": start + np.arange(values.shape[1]) * interval,
        "distance": ("distance", np.arange(values.shape[0]) * spacing, {"units": "m"}),
    },
    attrs={"data_category": "DAS"},
)
patch = dc.io.xarray_to_patch(array)
```

The distance origin here is relative to the first released channel. Data units remain unknown; the conversion does not assign strain or strain-rate units without source metadata. Choose the mapping from the release documentation rather than applying this layout to arbitrary HDF5 files.

A reduced AP Sensing release, such as the Cape Muroto tremor files, keeps the `DAQ`, `Metadata` and `DAS` groups but drops the version attributes, interrogator, time zone and data rate the AP Sensing reader needs, so it is not read automatically. Its 1,079 positions over about 55 km are spaced roughly ten times the stated `SpatialSampling`, and `DAQ/RepetitionFrequency` may or may not be the output rate. Read such a file with h5py as above, taking the time step and positions from the release's documentation.

## Research NetCDF files

NetCDF products that do not follow the CF conventions DASCore reads open with xarray and convert with `dascore.io.xarray_to_patch` once their variables are chosen and labelled. Keep each variable in its own patch, set units from the file's own description, and keep the time labels the file states. These examples use files from three published DTS datasets.

A temperature-by-depth record, where xarray decodes the CF time but the units need DASCore's spelling (Speulderbos soil temperature, `dts_data.nc`):

```{python}
#| eval: false
import xarray as xr

import dascore as dc

array = xr.open_dataset("dts_data.nc")["dts_temperature"]
array["depth"].attrs["units"] = "cm"
array.attrs = {"data_units": "degC", "data_type": "temperature"}
patch = dc.io.xarray_to_patch(array)
```

Separate up and down cable variables, as separate patches (EGS Collab, `AML_DTS.nc`, whose file-level `units` attribute is "degrees C"):

```{python}
#| eval: false
import xarray as xr

import dascore as dc

dataset = xr.open_dataset("AML_DTS.nc")
patches = []
for name in ("up_data", "down_data"):
    array = dataset[name]
    array["depth"].attrs["units"] = "m"
    array.attrs = {"data_units": "degC", "data_type": "temperature", "tag": name}
    patches.append(dc.io.xarray_to_patch(array))
spool = dc.spool(patches)
```

A statistics product with variable-specific units and MATLAB datenum times, here the temperature variance of the averaged cables (Helsinki SMEAR III, `DTS_statistics_SMEARIII_Karttunen_et_al.nc`):

```{python}
#| eval: false
import numpy as np
import xarray as xr

import dascore as dc

dataset = xr.open_dataset(
    "DTS_statistics_SMEARIII_Karttunen_et_al.nc", decode_times=False
)
array = dataset["var_av"]  # units "K**2"; each variable has its own
# MATLAB datenum counts days from 0000-01-00; day 719529 is 1970-01-01.
days = array["time"].values - 719529
time = np.datetime64("1970-01-01") + np.round(days * 86_400e3).astype("timedelta64[ms]")
array = array.assign_coords(time=time)
array.attrs = {"data_units": array.attrs["units"]}
patch = dc.io.xarray_to_patch(array)
```

Each statistic covers an averaging period the release documents; the time labels are as stated, not shifted to period centres.
